def angular_velocity(error, gain):
    """Image right is positive error. ROS left turn is positive angular speed."""
    return -gain * error

mission_1.program:
import cv2
import numpy as np

# The guide has loaded the selected photograph into image.
working = image.copy()
working = np.clip(working.astype(float) * 1.0 + 0, 0, 255).astype('uint8')
hsv = cv2.cvtColor(working, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)

lower = np.array([0, 0, 0])
upper = np.array([40, 210, 118])
raw_mask = cv2.inRange(hsv, lower, upper)

kernel = np.ones((3, 3), np.uint8)
opened = cv2.morphologyEx(raw_mask, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, kernel)

clean = cv2.morphologyEx(opened, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, kernel)

contours, hierarchy = cv2.findContours(
    clean, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
minimum_area = 3156
minimum_circularity = 0.1
contour_image = image.copy()
cv2.drawContours(contour_image, contours, -1, (255, 150, 0), 2)
rows = []
eligible = []
for index, contour in enumerate(contours):
    area = float(cv2.contourArea(contour))
    perimeter = cv2.arcLength(contour, True)
    circularity = 4 * np.pi * area / perimeter**2 if perimeter else 0
    moments = cv2.moments(contour)
    centroid = [moments['m10']/moments['m00'], moments['m01']/moments['m00']] if moments['m00'] else None
    passes = area >= minimum_area and circularity >= minimum_circularity
    rows.append(dict(candidate=index, area_px=area,
                     circularity=float(circularity), centroid=centroid, eligible=passes))
    x, y = contour[0, 0]
    cv2.putText(contour_image, str(index), (x, max(y, 15)),
                cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 0.45, (255, 80, 0), 1)
    if passes:
        eligible.append((area, index))

annotated = image.copy()
box = None
selected = None
if eligible:
    area, selected = max(eligible)
    box = cv2.boundingRect(contours[selected])
    x, y, width, height = box
    cv2.rectangle(annotated, (x, y), (x + width, y + height), (0, 220, 0), 2)
    center = (int(x + width / 2), int(y + height / 2))
    cv2.circle(annotated, center, 5, (0, 0, 255), -1)
    centroid = rows[selected]['centroid']
    if centroid:
        cv2.drawMarker(annotated, tuple(map(int, centroid)), (0, 255, 255), markerSize=12)
image_center_x = image.shape[1] // 2
cv2.line(annotated, (image_center_x, 0),
         (image_center_x, image.shape[0]), (255, 0, 255), 1)
detected = box is not None

responses.final.course_reflection:
This activity was pretty interesting in seeing how the robot took it's camera and connected it to movement, however I did run into a couple issues such as terminal 3 just never working in mission 2 and mission 3 where it would bring up the two windows but just did not show anything, when moving the terminal it would just take this weird screenshot of the virtual environment background as it's main window, it was just a bit weird so I didn't use it that much. Some other minor issues existed within this program, like mission 2 broke until I deleted the folder, I initially couldn't even open the Lab until I changed a piece of code in one of the files, the robot simulator when resetting it needed to be resumed because it just automatically went to pause upon reset, so I spent a while trying to figure that out.

Overall there were a lot of bug issues but other than that it wasn't bad, it taught me a lot about image processing and what we can do with it and keeps my motivation around generally the same where I don't see it as a full time career but may work on it as like a side project.
responses.final.synthesis: The 3 missions taught me how using visual evidence, we can determine how to identify objects through the use of colors/hues/saturation/brightness and how pixel's themselves cannot be used to identify what an object is and need some sort of category to be placed into. This was seen in the classical/learned detector comparison where the classical could select the object however did not give it a name because it just saw a general most grouped up pixels in the masking and created a box around it, with the learned detector however when there were no obstacles and was just a normal image it managed to identify which part of the mug was the cup and detect and identify it while cutting out the handle. The pillar centering mission explains how just detecting color can't be used to identify the object and distance of the object simply because different objects can have the same color, so just color alone won't cut out for which object it is if theres multiple obejcts that all have the same/similar colors. It also can't tell distance because it just show's which pixels are on screen, you can infer that the more pixels there are the closer an object is, but the object could also just be that big so it's unreliable. The line-following experiments are the final part where it includes robot movement on top of identifying a constantly changing image (the camera) it's basically the final connection where the robot takes a picture of the line it's currently on, then it adjusts it's turning to continue following this line without ever continuing off the line. A control choice for the images such as adding an obstacle for the learned detector cause the detector to not be able to identify the object at all, not even a general region showing that even a small obstacle could affect the final results super easily. Other limitations could be brightness, multiple objects with the same color, and slow reactions to sudden obstacles.
responses.line_following.comparison: Between the saved practice and the track attempts, the one setting that I changed is the gain where with a higher amount in both the line and the curved track they both tend to oscillate a lot non stop basically being the exact same, however with a slightly lower gain there is a more visible difference. The straight one does one slight turn based on the graph initially before smoothing out for the rest of the line indicating a straight line movement which is what it was doing, however for the curved sergment with the same gain, there were a lot more turns espcially tiny spikes when doing any lines that were not straight not just the turn's alone. The mask basically look the exact same with the practice being exactly and the curved track being slightly ahead when the gain was higher. The amount of oscillation is proof that the gain was changed because gain directly affects how strong the steering correction should be, the stronger it is the more it would've had to readjust.
responses.line_following.limits: One stop or failure from my attempts was when the robot didn't move at all after I ran the controller, I wasn't sure why initially but eventually found out the reason was because everytime the simulator is resetted it defaults to being paused as well. For a real delivery robot around people, some tests with actual moving objects that could cross into the path would be necessary because it should be able to stop ahead of time in case of an obstacle and either move around it or wait for it to cross before moving.
responses.mission_1.diagnosis: For normal_1 and independent_mug they both gave different results where normal_1 provided us with a box that did have a box on the mug, the detector selected this because it's morphology mask show's a very visible cup with handle shape while all the other spots are small noise values, making selection a lot easier. For the independent_mug however it failed to select the region, the reasoning for this is because my values mainly selected darker values so when the mask was created because of the darker values being selected, the shadow's on the cup were the only pixels that were made bright and everything else was dark leaving half the cup uncaptured. It then proceeded to only select the handle as it was disconnected from everything else.
responses.mission_1.limitations: Increasing the brightness value made the box select basically nothing, the mask also just became fully white. The reasoning for this is because when a higher brightness value is accepted pretty much everything on the image will have some brightness making it more suspectable to being captured. Limitations for a different cup or background are the the colors mainly where if the background matches the same shade as the cup or if they're both super bright like a white color.
responses.mission_2.choice: I believe the learned detector is better for further testing because it had better rates of identifying boxes and not giving out any false positives, In normal_1 the mask IoU looks over the entire mug with the handle included however with the learned version it specifically selects out the cup, whereas with classical it has a near perfect IoU however does not identify the mug as a cup/mug. A detailed foreground mask does not identify the requested mug because it only tells you which pixels are in the foreground, but it doesn't know which pixel is what, if the handle is the entire mug, if just the left side is a cup, etc. One important limit of this small image test is how it doesn't test other mugs with varying colors.
responses.mission_2.comparison: For a normal condition, classical had 2 correct boxes and 1 false box and 0 missed mugs, while learned had 2 correct boxes and 0 false boxes and 0 missed mugs. Dim condition had 0 correct boxes 2 false boxes  and 2 missed mugs for classical, and 2 correct boxes and 0 false boxes and 0 missed mugs for learned. Occluded for classical had 2 correct boxes 1 false box and 0 missed mugs, and learned had 0 correct boxes and 0 false boxes, with 2 missed mugs.  The main differences for locating the mug was definitely the occluded condition where the learned model struggled to identify the mug when there was an occlusion in both occluded 1 and occluded 2, there was no prediction from the learning model however with the classical model it did have a prediction but it did not identify the mug itself.
responses.pillar_search.diagnosis: 20261031T013349-b5f7fe79 was the attempt where it only looked at the blue pillar and it was relatively successful in the centering, it took it's camera and clearly identified the pillar with it's mask and then placed the yellow centroid very close to the magenta center line. Whenever I changed the setting values, I didn't see much changes when I messed around with the settings but this could be a testing error.
responses.pillar_search.evidence: For the four-color attempt, pretty much all the colors at some point were centered at some point based on the state timeline and camera evidence, it just took a while for each one of them because of the turning.  They were likely also not perfectly centered, probably the same with just the blue one where it was very close but the centroid and magenta line were just right next to each other. A centered colored region and a stable hold do not prove object identity or distance because with a centered colored region, it can detect that the color is near the center of the camera but different objects can have this same shape, with the stable hold the object remained in the detected space for a certain amount of time but it doesn't tell us how far it is because we're measuring with time of how long something is on the camera view instead of distance of how far something may be.
